contributions.headingText: Pyloric gland adenoma (PGA) of the gallbladder is a grossly visible non-invasive neoplasm of the gallbladder composed of uniform back-to-back mucinous glands arranged in a tubular configuration.
2E92.6 Benign neoplasm of gallbladder, extrahepatic bile ducts or ampulla of Vater
Acceptable: intracholecystic papillary-tubular neoplasm, gastric pyloric, simple mucinous type {22895264}.
There is no preferential localization within the gallbladder.

PGAs are found in 0.2–0.5% of gallbladders removed for cholelithiasis or chronic cholecystitis [[Albores-Saavedra J, Henson DE, Klimstra DS. Tumors of the gallbladder, extrahepatic bile ducts, and Vaterian system. Washington, DC: American Registry of Pathology; 2015. (AFIP atlas of tumor pathology, series 4; fascicle 23).]], and they account for about 10% of all grossly visible non-invasive neoplasms of the gallbladder {22895264}. They are more common in females, and most occur in adults {8416136; 9923922; 22386521}.

PGAs are often < 2 cm and asymptomatic, and they are usually discovered incidentally. However, when they arise in the gallbladder neck, they may lead to gallbladder distension and right upper quadrant pain {22895264} [[Albores-Saavedra J, Henson DE, Klimstra DS. Tumors of the gallbladder, extrahepatic bile ducts, and Vaterian system. Washington, DC: American Registry of Pathology; 2015. (AFIP atlas of tumor pathology, series 4; fascicle 23).]].

There are no well-established etiological factors for PGA. However, 50–65% of PGAs are associated with cholelithiasis {22386521}. Occasionally, they occur in association with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome {7003570} or familial adenomatous polyposis [[Albores-Saavedra J, Henson DE, Klimstra DS. Tumors of the gallbladder, extrahepatic bile ducts, and Vaterian system. Washington, DC: American Registry of Pathology; 2015. (AFIP atlas of tumor pathology, series 4; fascicle 23).]].

There are few data on pathogenesis. PGAs do not harbour TP53 or CDKN2A mutations, which are common in invasive carcinomas of the gallbladder {9923922}. Several studies have found immunohistochemical expression of β-catenin and mutations of CTNNB1 in 60% of PGAs {12023580; 11196159}, whereas mutations in CTNNB1 are found in < 10% of the carcinomas {11309300; 12023580}. These data suggest that the molecular pathology of PGAs differs from that of invasive carcinomas, and that PGA plays only a minor role in gallbladder carcinogenesis [[Albores-Saavedra J, Henson DE, Klimstra DS. Tumors of the gallbladder, extrahepatic bile ducts, and Vaterian system. Washington, DC: American Registry of Pathology; 2015. (AFIP atlas of tumor pathology, series 4; fascicle 23).]].
Some PGAs are sessile, whereas others are pedunculated {22895264}. The lesions are often readily detached from the mucosal surface and may be free-floating, mistaken as sludge in the lumen.

PGAs are composed of lobules of small, tightly packed, bland-looking pyloric-type or Brunner gland–like glands, some of which may be cystically dilated. The tumour cells reveal abundant apical mucinous cytoplasm, peripherally located nuclei, and a low N:C ratio. There is minimal or no intervening stroma {22895264; 22386521; 8950764; 1709553}. Paneth cells and neuroendocrine cells are often present. The uninvolved gallbladder mucosa is mostly devoid of dysplasia or pyloric gland metaplasia {22895264; 22386521; 8950764; 1709553}.

In the majority of the lesions, there is minimal cytological atypia, although the architecture is commonly complex. Foci of high-grade dysplasia may be seen in larger (> 1 cm) cases, which may occasionally even be associated with invasive carcinoma {21411787; 22386521; 22895264}.

The tumour cells are usually positive for CK7, and they diffusely and strongly express MUC6.

Pyloric gland metaplasia, when polypoid, can be confused with PGA; this appears to be the source of some controversy regarding the nature of these lesions in the literature {22895264}, because some major studies on adenomas have in fact predominantly involved subcentimetre foci of pyloric gland metaplasia {15332368; 16724345; 19476792}. Unlike PGA, pyloric gland metaplasia is often microscopic and not well demarcated from the surrounding mucosa. Therefore, pyloric gland nodules < 0.5 cm arising in a background of pyloric gland metaplasia in the adjacent mucosa should not be designated as PGA {22386521}.
PGAs are very rarely sampled by cytology.
Essential: non-invasive, benign glandular neoplasm of the gallbladder; usually composed of mucinous glands with pyloric or Brunner gland features.

PGAs with high-grade dysplasia are staged as pTis. If there is an associated invasive carcinoma, staging follows the protocol for carcinomas of the gallbladder [[Amin MB, Edge S, Greene F, et al., editors. AJCC cancer staging manual. 8th ed. New York (NY): Springer; 2017.]].

If invasive carcinoma is ruled out, PGAs are cured by cholecystectomy, even when high-grade dysplasia is present. The potential for multifocal biliary neoplasm as found in intracholecystic papillary neoplasms is not thought to be substantial for PGAs. The prognosis for PGAs with an associated invasive carcinoma probably depends on stage; however, the reported cases are too few to derive a conclusion {21411787; 22386521; 22895264}.
